newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to "teach lesson" to regional bosses.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to "teach lesson" to regional bosses.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, signalling a new focus on domestic policy, threatened on Friday to "slap the hands" of corrupt leaders in Russia's regions.
"I know there are a lot of bosses who got big powers and immediately opened up their own, big pockets," Yeltsin said in a regular radio address.

"They think they are far away from Moscow and there will be no control over them. They are wrong. We will start with checking their income and assets declarations and slap their hands to teach them a lesson."

Yeltsin, who says organised crime and corruption threaten the very existence of the state, has launched a high-profile anti-graft campaign. He has published a declaration of his own income and told all other senior officials to do the same.
As his pre-recorded radio address was broadcast, Yeltsin flew to Russia's second city St Petersburg for a one-day foray into high culture.
The trip is his first inside Russia since hectic campaigning last summer which won him a second term in office but overstrained his heart.
Yeltsin, 66, resumed active work earlier this year following an eight-month absence due to heart surgery and pneumonia.
He devoted most of May to foreign policy, signing deals with NATO and the former Soviet republics of Belarus and Ukraine.
He also signed a peace deal with Russia's separatist region of Chechnya, but said on Friday the time had come to concentrate on domestic issues.
"We need to work inside the country now," Yeltsin told reporters on arrival in St Petersburg.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky has said Yeltsin will sign a string of decrees in the city, which is home to some of Russia's greatest cultural treasures.
Some of them "will sound slightly unusual to Russian ears", Interfax news agency quoted Yastrzhembsky as saying, citing a possible decree "On St Petersburg as Russia's cultural capital".

Yeltsin is taking reform guru and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, who launched his political career in St Petersburg, and Economy Minister Yakov Urinson with him, hoping to jolt the former tsarist capital out of its provincial stagnation.
Consigned to second-rate status by the Bolsheviks, the city has failed since communism fell to live up to the vision of its 18th century founder Peter the Great as a "window on the West".
Now it is seeking to turn things around with a debut Eurobond to raise $300 million on international capital markets.
Yeltsin, a building engineer by training and not known for promoting the arts, will also chair a meeting of his Council on Culture and Art at the Russian Museum.

The museum, home to the biggest collection of Russian painting and, like all the arts, suffering from the cash squeeze which has accompanied Yeltsin's reforms, may get a cash pledge from the president in the tradition of his re-election drive.
The Kremlin leader said in his radio address the time has come to pay more attention to regional problems.

"The economic policy of the regions should be modern and competent, like in Moscow, Nizhny Novgorod and Novosibirsk," Yeltsin said in a reference to the most advanced Russian regions where reforms have started to bear fruit.
